## Definition

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open $C^2$ domain. Use the Cartesian gradient, divergence, row-component Jacobian, and componentwise Laplacian on $D$. For constants $\rho_0,\nu>0$, a body acceleration $f\in C(I\times D;\mathbb R^3)$, a velocity $w\in C^1(I;C^2(D;\mathbb R^3))$, and a scalar pressure $q\in C(I;C^1(D))$, define the full momentum residual

$$\mathcal R(w,q):=\partial_t w+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla q-\nu\Delta w-f.$$

The forced constant-density incompressible model is $\mathcal R(u,p)=0$ with $\operatorname{div}u=0$. A common-wall comparison consists of two divergence-free velocity fields $u,v$ in the displayed regularity class whose traces on $\partial D$ agree with the same prescribed boundary velocity $\gamma(t,\cdot)$. For a divergence-free comparison field $w$ with a different trace, a divergence-free wall lift is a field $\ell\in C^1(I;C^2(D;\mathbb R^3))$ with $\operatorname{div}\ell=0$ and $\ell|_{\partial D}=w|_{\partial D}-\gamma$; whenever such a lift is supplied, the corrected field is $v=w-\ell$ and its residual is $\mathcal R(v,q)$. This definition asserts no lift exists for arbitrary boundary data.

For a flat periodic channel $D_{\rm ch}=\mathbb T_{L_x}\times(0,h)\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$ and $L_x,L_z,h>0$, a specific tangential lift for lower and upper wall defects $a(t)e_x$ and $b(t)e_x$ is

$$\ell(t,x,y,z)=\bigl(a(t)(1-y/h)+b(t)y/h,\,0,\,0\bigr).$$

Here $e_x=(1,0,0)$, $a,b\in C^1(I,\mathbb R)$, and the channel is periodic in $x,z$ with physical walls $y=0,h$. This lift is defined only for the stated tangential wall-defect data.

For the capillary-gravity model, let $h,\rho,g,L_x,L_y>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, use horizontal coordinates $(x,y)\in\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}$ and vertical coordinate $z\in(-h,0)$, positive upward, with the flat mean surface at $z=0$. Let $\eta\in C^1(I;C^2(\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}))$ be surface elevation and $\phi\in C^1(I;C^2(\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times[-h,0]))$ a real velocity potential, so all displayed derivatives extend continuously to the top and bottom. Set $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2$ and $\Delta_H=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$. The capillary-gravity potential model is

$$\Delta\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$

$$\eta_t(t,x,y)=\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\qquad \phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\eta(t,x,y)-\frac{\sigma}{\rho}\Delta_H\eta(t,x,y)=0.$$

These are definitions of mathematical model interfaces. They assert neither existence of a solution for general data nor nonlinear free-surface or sharp-interface convergence. In the optional SI interpretation, $[x]=[y]=[z]=[h]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[\eta]=\mathrm m$, $[\phi]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[g]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[\sigma]=\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[f]=[\mathcal R]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $c$ with $c(n)\in X_n$. Let $T>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^2$ domain, let $I$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $\rho_0,\nu>0$. Suppose $u,v\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline D;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p,q\in C([0,T];C^1(\overline D))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of $\overline D$, with $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{div}v=0$. Let $f\in C([0,T]\times\overline D;\mathbb R^3)$, and for any velocity $w$ and scalar pressure $\pi$ set

$$\mathcal R(w,\pi):=\partial_tw+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla\pi-\nu\Delta w-f.$$

Assume $\mathcal R(u,p)=0$, and suppose $u$ and $v$ have the same boundary trace on $\partial D$ at each time. Define $r=\mathcal R(v,q)$.

the bilinear gradient norm

$$L(t)=\sup_{x\in\overline D}\ \sup_{|\xi|=|\zeta|=1}\left|\zeta\cdot D_xu(t,x)\xi\right|,$$

where $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$ is the row-component Jacobian and $\xi,\zeta$ are Euclidean unit vectors. For a vector field $F$, write $\|F\|_{L^2(D)}=(\int_D|F(x)|^2\,dx)^{1/2}$. Set $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$. Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|v(t)-u(t)\|_{L^2(D)}\le e^{A(t)}\left(\|v(0)-u(0)\|_{L^2(D)}+\int_0^t e^{-A(s)}\|r(s)\|_{L^2(D)}\,ds\right).$$

The same estimate holds on the flat periodic channel $D_{\rm ch}=\mathbb T_{L_x}\times(0,h)\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$, when the same equations and regularity assumptions hold, norms and integrals are over one periodic cell, and $u,v$ share the two wall traces; paired periodic-face terms cancel. In particular, let $w$ be smooth and divergence-free with traces $\gamma_0(t,x,z)+a(t)e_x$ at $y=0$ and $\gamma_h(t,x,z)+b(t)e_x$ at $y=h$, where $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$ are prescribed wall-velocity fields, while the exact solution $u$ has traces $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$. For $a,b\in C^1([0,T])$, set

$$\ell(t,x,y,z)=\bigl(a(t)(1-y/h)+b(t)y/h,\,0,\,0\bigr),\qquad v=w-\ell.$$

The corrected residual is

$$r_\ell=\mathcal R(v,q)=\mathcal R(w,q)-\ell_t-(\ell\cdot\nabla)w-(w\cdot\nabla)\ell+(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell+\nu\Delta\ell.$$

Thus $\|w(t)-u(t)\|_2\le\|\ell(t)\|_2+\|v(t)-u(t)\|_2$, with the preceding estimate applied to $v$ and $r_\ell$. This result assumes the displayed lift data and makes no general boundary-lifting claim, Prandtl-profile existence claim, or viscosity-uniform no-slip inviscid-limit claim. In SI units, $[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[p]=[q]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[f]=[r]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[a]=[b]=[\ell]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[h]=\mathrm m$, $L$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $A$ is dimensionless. Velocity, error and lift volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$; residual volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-2}}$, so their time-integrated contribution has units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The interval, domain, constants, fields, equations, common trace, and residual stated above. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for all $n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]] defines the full forced residual $\mathcal R(w,q)=w_t+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla q-\nu\Delta w-f$ with the Cartesian operators; the theorem's residual signs match that definition.

[F2] [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$, and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$.

[F3] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]: if $f,g\in L^2(D)$, then $\int_D|fg|\,dx\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums and products of differentiable real functions are differentiable, with $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and [[thm-chain-rule]]: $(\exp)'=\exp$, and differentiable real compositions obey $(f\circ g)'(t)=f'(g(t))g'(t)$ when the stated limit-point hypotheses hold.

[F6] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: if $G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and a Riemann-integrable $f$ agrees with $G'$ on $(a,b)$, then $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$.

[F7] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: every nonnegative real number has a unique nonnegative square root.

[F8] [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]: the norm from an inner product satisfies $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$; this applies to the real $L^2(D)$ inner product.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and definitions in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Put $e=v-u$ and $\pi=q-p$. Subtracting the exact equation for $u$ from the residual equation for $v$ gives $e_t+(v\cdot\nabla)e+(e\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla\pi-\nu\Delta e=r$, because $(v\cdot\nabla)v-(u\cdot\nabla)u=(v\cdot\nabla)e+(e\cdot\nabla)u$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 In the channel case, $\ell|_{y=0}=a e_x$, $\ell|_{y=h}=b e_x$, $\operatorname{div}\ell=0$, $\ell_t=(a'(1-y/h)+b'y/h)e_x$, $\Delta\ell=0$, and $(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell=0$, since $\ell$ depends only on $y$ in its first component and that component is affine in $y$. Thus $v=w-\ell$ is divergence-free and has the exact wall trace. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Set $Y(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$ and $R(t)=\|r(t)\|_2$. Pair the equation in step 1.1 with $e$ and integrate over $D$. The transport integral is $\frac12\int_D\operatorname{div}(v|e|^2)=0$ because $\operatorname{div}v=0$ and $e=0$ on $\partial D$; the pressure integral is $\rho_0^{-1}\int_D\operatorname{div}(\pi e)=0$ because $\operatorname{div}e=0$ and $e=0$ on $\partial D$; and the diffusion term is $-\nu\int_D e\cdot\Delta e=\nu\int_D|\nabla e|^2$ because $\int_D\operatorname{div}(\sum_i e_i\nabla e_i)=0$. These three identities use [F2]. The bilinear gradient norm gives $|(e\cdot\nabla)u\cdot e|\le L(t)|e|^2$, and [F3] gives $\int_D|e\cdot r|\le\sqrt{Y}R$. Pointwise in $x$, the difference quotients of $|e(t,x)|^2$ converge uniformly on $\overline D$ to $2e\cdot e_t$ as the time increment tends to zero, because $e,e_t$ are continuous on the compact space-time closure; integrating preserves this uniform limit since $D$ has finite volume. Therefore $Y'=2\int_D e\cdot e_t$ and $\frac12Y'(t)+\nu\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le L(t)Y(t)+R(t)\sqrt{Y(t)}$. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Expanding the convective term in $\mathcal R(w-\ell,q)$ gives $\mathcal R(w-\ell,q)=\mathcal R(w,q)-\ell_t-(\ell\cdot\nabla)w-(w\cdot\nabla)\ell+(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell+\nu\Delta\ell$. For this explicit lift, $(\ell\cdot\nabla)w=\ell_1\partial_xw$ and $(w\cdot\nabla)\ell=w_2(b-a)h^{-1}e_x$, while the last two lift-only terms vanish by step 1.2. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $\delta>0$, let $y_\delta(t)=\sqrt{Y(t)+\delta^2}$. The radicand is positive; the identity $|y_\delta(t+h)-y_\delta(t)|=|Y(t+h)-Y(t)|/(y_\delta(t+h)+y_\delta(t))$ first gives continuity of $y_\delta$, and the same difference-of-squares identity in the difference quotient gives $y_\delta'=Y'/(2y_\delta)$. Dropping the nonnegative diffusion term in step 2.1 and using $Y/y_\delta\le y_\delta$ and $\sqrt{Y}/y_\delta\le1$ yields $y_\delta'\le L y_\delta+R$. The function $L$ is continuous because $\overline D$ is compact and $D_xu$ is continuous; for $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$, the difference quotient is the average of $L$ on the interval between $t$ and $t+h$, so continuity gives $A'=L$. Thus [F4] and [F5] give $(e^{-A}y_\delta)'\le e^{-A}R$. Integrate on $[0,t]$ using [F6] and let $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the stated bound for $e=v-u$. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On the channel cell $[0,L_x]\times[0,h]\times[0,L_z]$, repeat the energy calculation in step 2.1 with $e=v-u$ and residual $r_\ell$ from step 2.2. For each of its divergence terms, integrate each coordinate derivative by the fundamental theorem [F6]: the paired $x$ and $z$ face values agree by periodicity, while the $y=0,h$ contributions vanish because $e=0$ at both walls. Thus the transport and pressure terms vanish and the diffusion term is $\nu\|\nabla e\|_2^2$, exactly as in step 2.1; no $C^2$ Euclidean boundary assertion about the rectangular cell is needed. The same norm regularization and integrating-factor argument in step 3.1 therefore gives the stated estimate for $v=w-\ell$ with residual $r_\ell$. Since $w-u=(v-u)+\ell$, [F8] gives $\|w-u\|_2\le\|v-u\|_2+\|\ell\|_2$, which is the asserted channel estimate. [given, F6, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $c$ with $c(n)\in X_n$. Let $T>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^2$ domain, let $I$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $\rho_0,\nu>0$. Suppose $u,v\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline D;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p,q\in C([0,T];C^1(\overline D))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of $\overline D$, with $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{div}v=0$. Let $f\in C([0,T]\times\overline D;\mathbb R^3)$, and for any velocity $w$ and scalar pressure $\pi$ set

$$\mathcal R(w,\pi):=\partial_tw+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla\pi-\nu\Delta w-f.$$

Assume $\mathcal R(u,p)=0$, and suppose $u$ and $v$ have the same boundary trace on $\partial D$ at each time. Define $r=\mathcal R(v,q)$.

Define the bilinear gradient norm

$$L(t)=\sup_{x\in\overline D}\ \sup_{|\xi|=|\zeta|=1}\left|\zeta\cdot D_xu(t,x)\xi\right|,$$

where $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$ is the row-component Jacobian and $\xi,\zeta$ are Euclidean unit vectors. For real vector fields $F,G\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^3)$, use the inner product $\langle F,G\rangle=\int_D F(x)\cdot G(x)\,dx$ and its norm $\|F\|_{L^2(D)}=(\int_D|F(x)|^2\,dx)^{1/2}$. Set $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$. Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|v(t)-u(t)\|_{L^2(D)}\le e^{A(t)}\left(\|v(0)-u(0)\|_{L^2(D)}+\int_0^t e^{-A(s)}\|r(s)\|_{L^2(D)}\,ds\right).$$

The same estimate holds on the flat periodic channel $D_{\rm ch}=\mathbb T_{L_x}\times(0,h)\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$, when the same equations and regularity assumptions hold, norms and integrals are over one periodic cell, and $u,v$ share the two wall traces; paired periodic-face terms cancel. In particular, let $w$ be smooth and divergence-free with traces $\gamma_0(t,x,z)+a(t)e_x$ at $y=0$ and $\gamma_h(t,x,z)+b(t)e_x$ at $y=h$, where $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$ are prescribed wall-velocity fields, while the exact solution $u$ has traces $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$. For $a,b\in C^1([0,T])$, set

$$\ell(t,x,y,z)=\bigl(a(t)(1-y/h)+b(t)y/h,\,0,\,0\bigr),\qquad v=w-\ell.$$

The corrected residual is

$$r_\ell=\mathcal R(v,q)=\mathcal R(w,q)-\ell_t-(\ell\cdot\nabla)w-(w\cdot\nabla)\ell+(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell+\nu\Delta\ell.$$

Thus $\|w(t)-u(t)\|_2\le\|\ell(t)\|_2+\|v(t)-u(t)\|_2$, with the preceding estimate applied to $v$ and $r_\ell$. This result assumes the displayed lift data and makes no general boundary-lifting claim, Prandtl-profile existence claim, or viscosity-uniform no-slip inviscid-limit claim. In SI units, $[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[p]=[q]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[f]=[r]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[a]=[b]=[\ell]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[h]=\mathrm m$, $L$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $A$ is dimensionless. Velocity, error and lift volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$; residual volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-2}}$, so their time-integrated contribution has units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$.

## Statement references

The forced constant-density incompressible operators and full residual convention: [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]].

The bounded $C^1$ divergence theorem used for the wall energy identity: [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]].

Bounded-domain energy estimates and their hypotheses: [Temam, §3.1, printed pp. 17–18 (PDF pp. 35–36)](https://ftp.mi.fu-berlin.de/pub/klima/NavierStokes/Temam-NavierStokesEquationsAndNonlinearFunctionalAnalysis.pdf).

Periodic relative-energy computation and the separate no-slip inviscid-limit boundary-layer condition: [Wiedemann, §§5.1–5.2, printed pp. 38–43](https://www.math.fau.de/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/wiedemann-NSE-final.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The interval, domain, constants, fields, equations, common trace, and residual stated above. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for all $n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]] defines the full forced residual $\mathcal R(w,q)=w_t+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla q-\nu\Delta w-f$ with the Cartesian operators; the theorem's residual signs match that definition.

[F2] [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$, and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] gives $|a\cdot b|\le|a||b|$ for $a,b\in\mathbb R^3$. The scalar inequality [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_D|fg|\,dx\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ for $f,g\in L^2(D)$. Consequently, applying it to the scalar magnitudes of vector fields gives $|\langle F,G\rangle|\le\int_D|F||G|\,dx\le\|F\|_2\|G\|_2$; bounded continuous fields on this finite-volume domain have these finite norms.

[F4] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums and products of differentiable real functions are differentiable, with $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and [[thm-chain-rule]]: $(\exp)'=\exp$, and differentiable real compositions obey $(f\circ g)'(t)=f'(g(t))g'(t)$ when the stated limit-point hypotheses hold.

[F6] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: if $G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and a Riemann-integrable $f$ agrees with $G'$ on $(a,b)$, then $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$.

[F7] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] states that $\mathbb R$ is a complete totally ordered field. Instantiate [[thm-of-square-roots]] with that field: every nonnegative real radicand has a unique nonnegative real square root, positive when the radicand is positive.

[F8] [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]: the norm from an inner product satisfies $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$; this applies to the real vector-field $L^2(D;\mathbb R^3)$ inner product specified above.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and definitions in the Statement and Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Put $e=v-u$ and $\pi=q-p$. Subtracting the exact equation for $u$ from the residual equation for $v$ gives $e_t+(v\cdot\nabla)e+(e\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla\pi-\nu\Delta e=r$, because $(v\cdot\nabla)v-(u\cdot\nabla)u=(v\cdot\nabla)e+(e\cdot\nabla)u$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 In the channel case, $\ell|_{y=0}=a e_x$, $\ell|_{y=h}=b e_x$, $\operatorname{div}\ell=0$, $\ell_t=(a'(1-y/h)+b'y/h)e_x$, $\Delta\ell=0$, and $(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell=0$, since $\ell$ depends only on $y$ in its first component and that component is affine in $y$. Thus $v=w-\ell$ is divergence-free and has the exact wall trace. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Set $Y(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$ and $R(t)=\|r(t)\|_2$. Pair the equation in step 1.1 with $e$ and integrate over $D$. The transport integral is $\frac12\int_D\operatorname{div}(v|e|^2)=0$ because $\operatorname{div}v=0$ and $e=0$ on $\partial D$; the pressure integral is $\rho_0^{-1}\int_D\operatorname{div}(\pi e)=0$ because $\operatorname{div}e=0$ and $e=0$ on $\partial D$; and the diffusion term is $-\nu\int_D e\cdot\Delta e=\nu\int_D|\nabla e|^2$ because $\int_D\operatorname{div}(\sum_i e_i\nabla e_i)=0$. These three identities use [F2]. The bilinear gradient norm gives $|(e\cdot\nabla)u\cdot e|\le L(t)|e|^2$, and the pointwise Euclidean bound followed by scalar Cauchy–Schwarz in [F3] gives $\int_D|e\cdot r|\le\int_D|e||r|\le\|e\|_2\|r\|_2=\sqrt{Y}R$. Pointwise in $x$, the difference quotients of $|e(t,x)|^2$ converge uniformly on $\overline D$ to $2e\cdot e_t$ as the time increment tends to zero, because $e,e_t$ are continuous on the compact space-time closure; integrating preserves this uniform limit since $D$ has finite volume. Therefore $Y'=2\int_D e\cdot e_t$ and $\frac12Y'(t)+\nu\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le L(t)Y(t)+R(t)\sqrt{Y(t)}$. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Expanding the convective term in $\mathcal R(w-\ell,q)$ gives $\mathcal R(w-\ell,q)=\mathcal R(w,q)-\ell_t-(\ell\cdot\nabla)w-(w\cdot\nabla)\ell+(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell+\nu\Delta\ell$. For this explicit lift, $(\ell\cdot\nabla)w=\ell_1\partial_xw$ and $(w\cdot\nabla)\ell=w_2(b-a)h^{-1}e_x$, while the last two lift-only terms vanish by step 1.2. [given, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For $\delta>0$, let $y_\delta(t)=\sqrt{Y(t)+\delta^2}$. The radicand is positive; the identity $|y_\delta(t+h)-y_\delta(t)|=|Y(t+h)-Y(t)|/(y_\delta(t+h)+y_\delta(t))$ first gives continuity of $y_\delta$, and the same difference-of-squares identity in the difference quotient gives $y_\delta'=Y'/(2y_\delta)$. Dropping the nonnegative diffusion term in step 2.1 and using $Y/y_\delta\le y_\delta$ and $\sqrt{Y}/y_\delta\le1$ yields $y_\delta'\le L y_\delta+R$. The function $L$ is continuous because $\overline D$ is compact and $D_xu$ is continuous; for $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$, the difference quotient is the average of $L$ on the interval between $t$ and $t+h$, so continuity gives $A'=L$. Thus [F4] and [F5] give $(e^{-A}y_\delta)'\le e^{-A}R$. Integrate on $[0,t]$ using [F6] and let $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the stated bound for $e=v-u$. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On the channel cell $[0,L_x]\times[0,h]\times[0,L_z]$, repeat the energy calculation in step 2.1 with $e=v-u$ and residual $r_\ell$ from step 2.2. For each of its divergence terms, integrate each coordinate derivative by the fundamental theorem [F6]: the paired $x$ and $z$ face values agree by periodicity, while the $y=0,h$ contributions vanish because $e=0$ at both walls. Thus the transport and pressure terms vanish and the diffusion term is $\nu\|\nabla e\|_2^2$, exactly as in step 2.1; no $C^2$ Euclidean boundary assertion about the rectangular cell is needed. The same norm regularization and integrating-factor argument in step 3.1 therefore gives the stated estimate for $v=w-\ell$ with residual $r_\ell$. Since $w-u=(v-u)+\ell$, [F8] gives $\|w-u\|_2\le\|v-u\|_2+\|\ell\|_2$, which is the asserted channel estimate. [given, F6, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $h,g,\rho,k,L_y>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, and $a\in\mathbb R$. Set $\lambda=2\pi/k$ and $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$; use horizontal coordinates $(x,y)\in\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}$ and vertical coordinate $z\in[-h,0]$, positive upward, with the mean surface at $z=0$. Define

$$\omega_\sigma=\sqrt{\left(gk+\frac{\sigma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh)},\qquad G(z)=\frac{\cosh(k(z+h))}{\cosh(kh)},\qquad \theta_\sigma=kx-\omega_\sigma t.$$

Let $S,C:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be the real sine and cosine functions. The fields

$$\eta_\sigma(t,x,y)=aC(\theta_\sigma),\qquad \phi_\sigma(t,x,y,z)=\frac{a\omega_\sigma}{k\tanh(kh)}G(z)S(\theta_\sigma)$$

are smooth, independent of $y$, periodic with horizontal periods $\lambda,L_y$, and solve exactly the linear capillary-gravity potential equations

$$\Delta\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$

$$\eta_t(t,x,y)=\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\qquad \phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\eta(t,x,y)-\frac{\sigma}{\rho}\Delta_H\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$

where $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2$ and $\Delta_H=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$. Here $h$ is depth, $g$ gravitational acceleration, $\rho$ constant density, $\sigma$ surface tension, and $\Delta_H$ is the horizontal Laplacian. In particular, the positive frequency obeys

$$\omega_\sigma^2=\left(gk+\frac{\sigma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh).$$

At $\sigma=0$ this mode is exactly the finite-depth gravity-wave mode. For any $T>0$, let $\eta\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}))$ and $\phi\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times[-h,0]))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of the closed slab and satisfy the same equations. Define the energy in one horizontal cell by

$$E(t)=\frac{\rho}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\int_{-h}^0 (|\phi_x|^2+|\phi_y|^2+|\phi_z|^2)\,dz\,dx\,dy+\frac{\rho g}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\eta^2\,dx\,dy+\frac{\sigma}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda (|\eta_x|^2+|\eta_y|^2)\,dx\,dy.$$

Then $E(t)$ is nonnegative and constant on $[0,T]$. These are exact deductions within the stated linear model; they do not assert a nonlinear free-surface solution, a sharp-interface convergence theorem, or an experimental observation. In SI units, $[h]=[L_y]=\mathrm m$, $[g]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\sigma]=\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, $[k]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[a]=[\eta]=\mathrm m$, $[\omega_\sigma]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $[\phi]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[E]=\mathrm J$ for the chosen finite transverse span.

## Statement references

Finite-depth gravity-capillary boundary conditions, hyperbolic vertical profile, and dispersion derivation: [MIT 18.357, Chapter 19, printed pp. 78–79 (PDF pp. 78–79)](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-357-interfacial-phenomena-fall-2010/04759cfc15c79928ca9f72a18b3864dd_MIT18_357F10_lec_all.pdf).

Independent surface-tension pressure derivation and deep-water gravity-capillary relation: [ETH Zürich, Mechanics of Continuous Media, lecture 23, printed pp. 185–187 (PDF pp. 5–7)](https://edu.itp.phys.ethz.ch/fs14/MechOfCont/lec23.pdf).

Independent gravity-capillary dispersion context and finite-depth gravity relation: [Firing, OCN 620, §19.4](https://uhslc.soest.hawaii.edu/ocn620/notes/surface-waves-1.html).

Finite-depth gravity-wave mode used at zero surface tension: [[thm-fd-x03]].

Model equations and conventions: [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive parameters, horizontal periods, smooth fields, and linear boundary equations in the Statement.

[A1] The capillary-gravity potential model is the mathematical model defined in [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]]: harmonic potential in $-h<z<0$, impermeable bottom, kinematic condition $\eta_t=\phi_z$ at $z=0$, and dynamic condition $\phi_t+g\eta-(\sigma/\rho)\Delta_H\eta=0$.

[F1] [[thm-fd-x03]]: for $h,g,k>0$, $\omega_0=\sqrt{gk\tanh(kh)}>0$ and the fields $\eta_0=aC(kx-\omega_0t')$, $\phi_0=(ag/\omega_0)G(z)S(kx-\omega_0t')$ solve the finite-depth linear gravity-wave system; $G(z)=\cosh(k(z+h))/\cosh(kh)$.

[F2] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: every nonnegative real number has a unique nonnegative square root.

[F3] [[thm-chain-rule]]: if differentiable real functions are composed at points satisfying its limit-point hypotheses, then $(f\circ g)'= (f'\circ g)g'$.

[F4] [[cor-greens-first-identity-for-glued-elementary-solid-regions]]: for a finite gluing $E$ of elementary solid regions, $u\in C^1$ and $v\in C^2$ on an open neighborhood, $\iiint_E(\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle+u\Delta v)=\iint_{\partial E}u\langle\nabla v,n\rangle$.

[F5] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: differentiable products satisfy $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.

[F6] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]: if $g,h$ are continuous on a compact rectangle and $\partial_x g=h$ in the interior, the parameter integral of $g$ is differentiable and its derivative is the corresponding integral of $h$.

## Proof

**Given:** The assumptions above, with $\sigma\ge0$ and positive $h,g,\rho,k$.

1.1 Let $\omega_0=\sqrt{gk\tanh(kh)}>0$ and let $c_\sigma=\sqrt{1+\sigma k^2/(\rho g)}>0$, whose existence and positivity follow from [F1] and [F2]. Set $\omega=c_\sigma\omega_0$. Then $\omega^2=(1+\sigma k^2/(\rho g))gk\tanh(kh)=(gk+\sigma k^3/\rho)\tanh(kh)$, and the radicand in the Statement is positive, so its positive square root is this $\omega$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Write $\theta_0(t',x)=kx-\omega_0t'$, and take the gravity mode $\eta_0,\phi_0$ from [F1]. Define $t'=c_\sigma t$, $\eta(t,x,y)=\eta_0(t',x,y)$, and $\phi(t,x,y,z)=c_\sigma\phi_0(t',x,y,z)$. The chain rule [F3] gives $\eta_t=c_\sigma(\eta_0)_{t'}=c_\sigma(\phi_0)_z=\phi_z$; harmonicity and the bottom condition persist because this transformation only rescales time and amplitude. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $Q=[0,\lambda]\times[0,L_y]\times[-h,0]$. Apply [F6] successively to the rectangular cell integrals and use [F5] to differentiate the squared gradients; the fields and time derivatives are continuous on the compact cell, so the hypotheses hold. Apply [F4] with $u=\phi_t$ and $v=\phi$. The interior term $\phi_t\Delta\phi$ vanishes; opposite periodic faces cancel; the bottom term vanishes by $\phi_z(-h)=0$. Hence $K'(t)=\rho\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda \phi_t(t,x,y,0)\phi_z(t,x,y,0)\,dx\,dy$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.4 Differentiate the two surface terms in $E$ using [F5] and [F6]. For the gradient term apply [F4] on $Q$ to $u=\eta_t(x,y)$ and $v=\eta(x,y)$, extended constantly in $z$; the top and bottom normal derivatives vanish and the paired periodic-face terms cancel. Dividing the identity by $h$ gives $\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\nabla_H\eta\cdot\nabla_H\eta_t\,dx\,dy=-\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\eta_t\Delta_H\eta\,dx\,dy$, so $V'(t)=\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda(\rho g\eta-\sigma\Delta_H\eta)\eta_t\,dx\,dy$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 The gravity mode is independent of $y$, so $\Delta_H\eta_0=-k^2\eta_0$. Its gravity dynamic condition is $(\phi_0)_{t'}+g\eta_0=0$. Therefore $\phi_t+g\eta-(\sigma/\rho)\Delta_H\eta=c_\sigma^2(\phi_0)_{t'}+g\eta_0+(\sigma k^2/\rho)\eta_0=(-g c_\sigma^2+g+\sigma k^2/\rho)\eta_0=0$, since $c_\sigma^2=1+\sigma k^2/(\rho g)$. Thus the transformed fields satisfy the capillary dynamic condition. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Since $\omega=c_\sigma\omega_0$ and $\omega_0^2=gk\tanh(kh)$, the coefficient of $G(z)S(\theta_\sigma)$ in $\phi=c_\sigma\phi_0(c_\sigma t)$ is $agc_\sigma/\omega_0=a\omega/(k\tanh(kh))$. Also $\theta_0(c_\sigma t,x)=\theta_\sigma$. This proves the displayed mode formula, including $a=0$. At $\sigma=0$, $c_\sigma=1$ and the same formulas are exactly the gravity mode [F1]. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The kinematic condition makes $\phi_z(t,x,y,0)=\eta_t$. The dynamic condition makes $\rho\phi_t+\rho g\eta-\sigma\Delta_H\eta=0$. Adding the derivatives in steps 1.3 and 1.4 therefore gives $E'(t)=K'(t)+V'(t)=0$. Each term in $E$ is nonnegative because $\rho,g>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, so $E$ is nonnegative and constant on $[0,T]$. [given, A1, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $h,g,\rho,k,L_y>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, and $a\in\mathbb R$. Set $\lambda=2\pi/k$ and $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$; use horizontal coordinates $(x,y)\in\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}$ and vertical coordinate $z\in[-h,0]$, positive upward, with the mean surface at $z=0$. Let $S,C:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be real sine and cosine. For $x\in\mathbb T_\lambda$, choose any representative $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R$. Define

$$\omega_\sigma=\sqrt{\left(gk+\frac{\sigma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh)},\qquad G(z)=\frac{\cosh(k(z+h))}{\cosh(kh)},\qquad \theta_\sigma=k\widetilde x-\omega_\sigma t.$$

Only $S(\theta_\sigma)$ and $C(\theta_\sigma)$ are used: changing $\widetilde x$ by $n\lambda$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, changes the real phase by $2\pi n$ and leaves these values unchanged. Thus the formulas below define fields on the torus rather than a globally real-valued phase there. The fields

$$\eta_\sigma(t,x,y)=aC(\theta_\sigma),\qquad \phi_\sigma(t,x,y,z)=\frac{a\omega_\sigma}{k\tanh(kh)}G(z)S(\theta_\sigma)$$

are smooth, independent of $y$, periodic with horizontal periods $\lambda,L_y$, and solve exactly the linear capillary-gravity potential equations

$$\Delta\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$

$$\eta_t(t,x,y)=\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\qquad \phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\eta(t,x,y)-\frac{\sigma}{\rho}\Delta_H\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$

where $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2$ and $\Delta_H=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$. Here $h$ is depth, $g$ gravitational acceleration, $\rho$ constant density, $\sigma$ surface tension, and $\Delta_H$ is the horizontal Laplacian. In particular, the positive frequency obeys

$$\omega_\sigma^2=\left(gk+\frac{\sigma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh).$$

At $\sigma=0$ this mode is exactly the finite-depth gravity-wave mode. For any $T>0$, let $\eta\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}))$ and $\phi\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\mathbb T_\lambda\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times[-h,0]))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of the closed slab and satisfy the same equations. Define the energy in one horizontal cell by

$$E(t)=\frac{\rho}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\int_{-h}^0 (|\phi_x|^2+|\phi_y|^2+|\phi_z|^2)\,dz\,dx\,dy+\frac{\rho g}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda\eta^2\,dx\,dy+\frac{\sigma}{2}\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda (|\eta_x|^2+|\eta_y|^2)\,dx\,dy.$$

Then $E(t)$ is nonnegative and constant on $[0,T]$. These are exact deductions within the stated linear model; they do not assert a nonlinear free-surface solution, a sharp-interface convergence theorem, or an experimental observation. In SI units, $[h]=[L_y]=\mathrm m$, $[g]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\sigma]=\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, $[k]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[a]=[\eta]=\mathrm m$, $[\omega_\sigma]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $[\phi]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[E]=\mathrm J$ for the chosen finite transverse span.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The positive parameters, horizontal periods, smooth fields, and linear boundary equations in the Statement.

[A1] The capillary-gravity potential model is the mathematical model defined in [[def-fd-wall-defect-capillary-models]]: harmonic potential in $-h<z<0$, impermeable bottom, kinematic condition $\eta_t=\phi_z$ at $z=0$, and dynamic condition $\phi_t+g\eta-(\sigma/\rho)\Delta_H\eta=0$.

[F1] [[thm-fd-x03]]: for $h,g,k>0$, $\omega_0=\sqrt{gk\tanh(kh)}>0$ and the fields $\eta_0=aC(kx-\omega_0t')$, $\phi_0=(ag/\omega_0)G(z)S(kx-\omega_0t')$ solve the finite-depth linear gravity-wave system; $G(z)=\cosh(k(z+h))/\cosh(kh)$.

[F6] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]: if $g,h$ are continuous on a compact rectangle and $\partial_x g=h$ in the interior, the parameter integral of $g$ is differentiable and its derivative is the corresponding integral of $h$.

**Given:** The assumptions above, with $\sigma\ge0$ and positive $h,g,\rho,k$.

[given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 First, [F7] and repeated differentiation show that every derivative of $S,C$ is one of $S,C,-S,-C$, and every derivative of $\sinh,\cosh$ alternates between those two continuous functions. All four functions are therefore $C^\infty$. By [F3] and [F5], compositions with the affine phases and products with $G(z)$ are smooth on real coordinates, extending across both vertical endpoints; the denominator $\cosh(kh)$ is a fixed positive number. The $2\pi$-periodicity in [F7] makes the formulas unchanged under $\widetilde x\mapsto\widetilde x+n\lambda$ for every integer $n$, and independence of $y$ gives period $L_y$. Hence the smooth formulas and all their derivatives descend to the horizontal torus. Write $\theta_0(t',\widetilde x)=k\widetilde x-\omega_0t'$, and take the gravity mode $\eta_0,\phi_0$ from [F1]. Define $t'=c_\sigma t$, $\eta(t,x,y)=\eta_0(t',x,y)$, and $\phi(t,x,y,z)=c_\sigma\phi_0(t',x,y,z)$. The chain rule [F3] gives $\eta_t=c_\sigma(\eta_0)_{t'}=c_\sigma(\phi_0)_z=\phi_z$; harmonicity and the bottom condition persist because this transformation only rescales time and amplitude. [given, F1, F3, F5, F7, algebra]

1.3 Let $Q=[0,\lambda]\times[0,L_y]\times[-h,0]$. Apply [F6] successively to the rectangular cell integrals and use [F5] to differentiate the squared gradients; the fields and time derivatives are continuous on the compact cell, so the hypotheses hold. Apply [F4] with $u=\phi_t$ and $v=\phi$. The interior term $\phi_t\Delta\phi$ vanishes; opposite periodic faces cancel; the bottom term vanishes by $\phi_z(-h)=0$. Hence $K'(t)=\rho\int_0^{L_y}\int_0^\lambda \phi_t(t,x,y,0)\phi_z(t,x,y,0)\,dx\,dy$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.4 Differentiate the two surface terms in $E$ using [F5] and [F6]. For the gradient term apply [F4] on $Q$ to $u=\eta_t(x,y)$ and $v=\eta(x,y)$, extended constantly in $z$; the top and bottom normal derivatives vanish and the paired periodic-face terms cancel. 2.2 Since $\omega=c_\sigma\omega_0$ and $\omega_0^2=gk\tanh(kh)$, the coefficient of $G(z)S(\theta_\sigma)$ in $\phi=c_\sigma\phi_0(c_\sigma t)$ is $agc_\sigma/\omega_0=a\omega/(k\tanh(kh))$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The kinematic condition makes $\phi_z(t,x,y,0)=\eta_t$. The dynamic condition makes $\rho\phi_t+\rho g\eta-\sigma\Delta_H\eta=0$.
